You can change almost every value of the virtual bass yourself.
Depending on the values the sound may distort or get louder; there is no liability for the result.
The tags next to each description are the evidence: research · manufacturer data · measured (on which phone) · estimate.
One \"reset to defaults\" always brings everything back. The output limit that protects your ears cannot be turned off.

Accuracy is not guaranteed, but these values were actually measured on this phone several times with a measurement microphone (UMIK-1).
Resets every value and turns developer mode off.
With per-harmonic envelope on, its own envelope (10/70 ms) is used instead of attack and release.
Attack and release only act on the P1-family models.

Sound below this frequency is treated as \"bass the speaker cannot play\" and turned into harmonics.
More bass (bass guitar, low vocals) becomes harmonics. If sounds that were heard well get changed too, it can get muddy.
Only the really low sounds (kick, 808) are used. The effect gets smaller.
The lowest note a speaker can play differs between phones; usually between 100 and 200 Hz.
The generated harmonics are played only within this range.
Harmonics the speaker cannot play are dropped, so less power is wasted and buzz may drop.
The generated harmonics are played only within this range.
Higher harmonics are heard too, so the pitch gets clearer, but it may get rough.
Cuts the original bass the speaker cannot play.
The speaker does not shake needlessly, so buzz drops and the amplifier protects less often. Too high and the body gets thin.
More of the original bass stays, but most of it is not heard and only uses power.
Twice the fundamental. Sounds the fullest, but with a low fundamental it also falls where the speaker cannot play.
Higher orders sound more natural a little lower. A harmonic the model leaves out (such as the 2nd of a low note) does not appear when raised.
Falls where most phone speakers play well, so it gives the bass the most presence. Too high and it hums.
Higher orders sound more natural a little lower.

Higher orders sound more natural a little lower.
Makes the pitch clearer, but too much sounds rough and metallic.
Higher orders sound more natural a little lower.
How fast the higher harmonics get quieter.
(steeper) A soft, round bass. Too steep and the effect almost disappears.
(gentler) Clearer and firmer, but it may get rough.
Research used 3 to 10 dB per octave.
How much harmonics long bass notes (bass lines) get.
The sustained method smears sound a little; a kick left to it may sound like \"boooom…\" instead of \"thump!\".
How much harmonics short bass hits (kicks) get.
Kicks get firmer. Too high and every hit may buzz.
How fast the harmonics follow when a bass note starts.
Kicks get firmer. Too short and every start may click.
How fast the harmonics fade when a bass note ends.
The bass lingers and sounds fuller, but fading after the original sound leaves a \"boooom\" tail.
Stops sharply like the original. Too short and the bass may sound shaky.
Holds down moments when the harmonics jump up suddenly.
Buzz at the start of a kick may drop. The first hit gets a little weaker.
Holds down fast wobbling of the harmonic level.
A \"hum-hum\" wobble may drop. For about 0.5 s after a sound starts the harmonics are quieter.
Joins the level changes of each harmonic into one, so they cut out and back in less often.
The virtual bass is 2 dB lower to make up for it. Switching it briefly interrupts the sound.
Works only with the P1 model.
The level of all generated harmonics.
The bass gets richer, but past a point it does not get louder; only buzz and pushed-down mids grow.
Because of the phone amplifier protection, the same strength reaches the limit sooner at higher volume.
Lowers the strength automatically as the volume rises, starting at this volume.
Starts reducing at a lower volume, so buzz drops.
Phone amplifiers limit their output by volume and battery state; that is also why the bass is weaker on a low battery.
How much the strength drops per 1% of volume.
Reduces more as the volume rises.
The most the volume link takes off.
Can reduce more at very high volume.
Briefly lowers the harmonics while the mids and highs are dense.
Fine buzz when many instruments play at once may drop. The bass gets a little weaker at that moment.
Virtual bass for small speakers usually sets the boundary \"the speaker cannot play below this\" (cut-off) between 100 and 200 Hz.
On the S26 Ultra the output falls steeply below 150-180 Hz. The default of 190 Hz comes from this measurement.
The harmonic band usually runs from the cut-off to about four times it.
On the S26 Ultra changes above 400 Hz made no audible difference.
Virtual bass for small speakers cuts the original sound at the cut-off frequency.
Smart amplifiers limit the output in real time so the diaphragm does not move too far.
How much the body thins out differs between phones. Not confirmed yet.
Pitch is mostly set by the 1st to 5th harmonics, and three harmonics are already enough for the effect.
On the Galaxy S26 Ultra too much at 220-400 Hz caused a \"koo-hoong\" noise.
The effect of each order on its own is not confirmed yet.
One study limited the harmonic levels to between 3 and 10 dB per octave.
On the S26 Ultra changes above 400 Hz were not audible, so this value had little effect.
A phase vocoder smears transients and nonlinear methods handle them well; a hybrid that splits the two was rated better.
The kick tail was confirmed on the S26 Ultra.
An expectation from general dynamics processing. Check it on the time graph.
On the S26 Ultra kicks blurred when the layer faded 40-60 ms after the dry sound.
The general statements beyond that are estimates.
Slightly better in listening rounds 7 and 8 on the S26 Ultra.
In the offline processing of listening round 6 on the S26 Ultra the wobble disappeared. The app version works differently and is not confirmed yet.
Ported from offline research processing. The effect in the app is not confirmed yet.
There is a clear trade-off between the amount of bass enhancement and quality: the more you add, the more distortion is heard.
The phone smart amplifier limits its output to protect the diaphragm and against heat.
On the S26 Ultra +3 to +4 was cleaner than +6.
The amplifier has a battery-tracking limiter and diaphragm protection.
On the S26 Ultra the bass protection threshold was about -27 dBFS at 80% volume and about -15 dBFS at 50%. The volume link reduced the buzz a lot.
An expectation from intermodulation: when strong bass moves the diaphragm, the mids and highs distort with it.
In listening round 19 on the S26 Ultra it could not be told apart from a fixed average level.
Moves the virtual-bass strength table to the lowest note this speaker plays. 150 Hz is the S26 Ultra as it is.
Higher notes (150-250 Hz) get harmonics too. The harmonics of very low notes (55-100 Hz) get smaller.
The other way round: low notes get bigger harmonics, higher notes are left empty.
The virtual-bass strength table was made for the S26 Ultra\'s speaker (floor 150 Hz). On other phones the table moves by that phone\'s floor.
Whether a moved table sounds as strong as on the S26 Ultra is still being checked. The strength comparison in \"Bass fit\" closes that gap by ear.

The microphone clipped. Turn the volume down a little.

The phone\'s microphone measures the speaker right next to it. Bars are relative to the loudest part. Below 100 Hz it hears less than is there, and body vibration can mix in. Virtual bass and EQ are off while it measures. Nothing is applied.

The microphone response the phone declares is taken off and the level turned into dB SPL with its sensitivity (unprocessed recording). Component values: a few dB off is possible. Above 5 kHz the direction of the sound changes a lot.
The microphone response the phone declares is taken off. The sensitivity is unknown, so the levels are in dBFS.
The microphone response the phone declares is taken off. Voice recognition recording does not match the sensitivity, so the levels are in dBFS.
This phone declares no microphone data, so the levels are uncorrected dBFS. Treble may look louder than it is.
As the microphone records it, uncorrected (dBFS). Phone microphones often record treble louder than it is.
